pathway.title: CHS INC — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: CHS Inc. entered fiscal 2027 with year-end total debt of USD 2,501.7 million against derived EBITDA of USD 1,969.5 million, a ratio of 1.27x, compared with 2.12x a year earlier (CP-1 C5). The improvement is real but partly seasonal, which the annual figure hides: the fall in total debt of USD 486.6 million, from USD 2,988.3 million, came entirely from notes payable, which fell by USD 703.5 million while long-term debt rose by USD 216.9 million (CP-1A D6), and on a last-twelve-months basis total debt over derived EBITDA was 2.53x, 2.92x and 2.57x at the three interim quarter ends (CP-1 C14). Leverage at the working capital peak is therefore 2.92x, not the 1.27x of the year-end balance sheet.

Earnings improved sharply and narrowly. Pretax income rose to USD 1,128.7 million from USD 614.8 million, and Energy alone moved from a loss of USD 19.0 million to earnings of USD 554.6 million, more than the group improvement of USD 513.9 million (CP-1 C16). Within Energy, the sources identify wider crack spreads and crude discounts, higher throughput, and a small refinery exemption benefit of approximately USD 205.0 million that management says only partially offsets total renewable fuel compliance costs and may not recur (CP-1A, 10-K page:64). Equity income was USD 569.2 million, 50.4% of pretax income (CP-2 E7), of which CF Nitrogen provided USD 406.3 million and USD 447.3 million of cash distributions. The fourth quarter derived from audited year less nine months carried USD 739.3 million of pretax income, and the annual report's own quarterly table disagrees with that split (CP-1A conflicts), so the phasing of the recovery is unverified while the annual totals stand.

Cash generation is strong in fiscal 2026 and not flattered by working capital. Operating cash flow was USD 1,584.0 million after a USD 184.0 million net working capital outflow (CP-2 E6), free cash flow after major maintenance was USD 1,052.5 million, and after preferred dividends and owner distributions it was USD 753.4 million (CP-1 C3, C4). This corrects CP-1A, which described operating cash flow as helped by working capital timing. In fiscal 2025 free cash flow after distributions was negative USD 1,120.9 million, so cash generation moved by USD 1,874.3 million between adjacent years (CP-2 E11).

Fixed charges are covered but the margin depends on the earnings base. EBITDA covers cash interest plus preferred dividends 5.87x in fiscal 2026 against 4.47x in fiscal 2025, and on the narrower operating EBITDA measure the cover is 3.78x against 2.35x (CP-2 E1, E2). Adding operating lease liabilities of USD 237.5 million gives 1.39x leverage, and treating the preferred stock at its redemption value of USD 2,273.3 million as a debt-like fixed claim gives 2.42x (CP-2 E3, E4), an analytical adjustment and not a statement of legal ranking.

The forward funding position is adequate but not abundant. Identified fiscal 2027 demands of USD 1,536.1 million comprise capital expenditures of USD 850.8 million, major maintenance of USD 41.8 million, preferred dividends of USD 168.7 million, owner cash returns of USD 315.0 million on the filing figures, scheduled long-term debt maturities of USD 58.6 million and interest on long-term debt of USD 101.3 million (CP-2 E5). That is close to fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,584.0 million, so a repeat of fiscal 2026 funds the plan almost exactly, and any shortfall would fall on the USD 2,800.0 million revolver, which is USD 1.40 of capacity for every USD 1.00 of the largest quarter-end notes payable balance of USD 1,995.1 million (CP-2 E8), or on the board's discretion over owner payments. Two announced projects of USD 450 million and USD 700 million are additional and unfunded in the sources.

What cannot be concluded: covenant headroom, because the net worth and ratio tests are described but no level is printed; the effect of letters of credit on revolver availability; structural position of creditors, because guarantors and security are not stated; and ratings and market pricing, which are out of scope.

runs.text: Strengths. First, balance sheet and liquidity: year-end leverage of 1.27x, USD 263.6 million of unrestricted cash and USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver to 2028-04-21 give CHS Inc. a liquidity base of about USD 3,063.6 million gross of letters of credit that are not supplied (CP-1, CP-2 E9). Second, debt profile: the long-term debt is unsecured private placement notes and a USD 300.0 million term loan, with USD 899.3 million, 44.9% of the total, maturing in the five fiscal years to 2031 and the largest single year at USD 450.0 million (CP-2 E10). Third, a discretionary distribution lever: the board decides the cash portion of patronage and the level of equity redemptions, and cash patronage paid fell from USD 300.4 million to USD 30.0 million between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026, so a stress case can release cash without a default event (CP-1A). Fourth, diversification across Energy, Grains and Agronomy, a financing arm and two minority joint ventures. Fifth, demonstrated cash support from CF Nitrogen of USD 447.3 million of distributions in fiscal 2026.

Weaknesses. First, thin and volatile operating earnings: operating earnings were USD 591.9 million on revenues of USD 39,231.2 million, a margin of 1.5%, and USD 90.8 million in fiscal 2025, so pretax income relies on equity income and other income (CP-1). Second, policy and spread dependence in Energy, where the largest blending obligation ever issued, open-market RIN purchases and a refinery exemption that may not recur all decide margin. Third, concentration: CF Nitrogen provides 71% of equity income (CP-1A D3), a non-controlled venture whose distributions follow nitrogen prices. Fourth, a working capital model that takes quarter-end leverage to 2.92x and ties up large inventory and receivables, with derivative liabilities of USD 546.6 million at year end against USD 178.0 million a year earlier, a mechanic for margin and liquidity calls if commodity prices spike, which the sources do not quantify (CP-1). Fifth, unverifiable structure and covenants: no agreement is supplied. Sixth, growth capital: expected capital expenditure of USD 850.8 million in fiscal 2027 against USD 463.3 million in fiscal 2026 plus two projects with no stated funding. Seventh, a small related-party exposure of USD 10.3 million past due from a director's farm, under Audit Committee-approved terms (CP-1A).

runs.text: No acquisition, sponsor transaction, merger or change of control is described in the sources, and the context lists no deal terms, so there is no transaction to summarize beyond the financing and project events below, each dated and classed by status. In fiscal 2026 the company issued no new notes: the debt table shows only the scheduled repayment of an 80,000 note and the sources state that "We repaid approximately $80.6 million and $331.6 million, respectively, of long-term debt consisting of scheduled debt maturities" for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2025 (10-K page:164). The one new long-term borrowing was the drawing of the revolving term loan: in the third quarter report the company states "we drew $300.0 million on our revolving term loan facility (the "Facility") for long-term capital planning purposes and utilized the proceeds to reduce short-term amounts outstanding" (10-Q Q3 page:13). That facility is fully drawn, its revolving period ends 2026-10-29 and it then becomes a nonrevolving term loan payable 2029-10-29 (10-K page:165); the scheduled reversion is a subsequent event after the fiscal year end that no later document confirms. On 2026-08-26 the securitization and repurchase facilities were extended to 2027-08-25 (10-K page:164). These are completed events, not proposals. Two announced projects are proposed and conditional: a phosphate production facility of nearly 450 million in Louisiana in a joint venture with OCP North America, and a soybean processing facility of approximately 700 million in Evansville, Wisconsin, with the release stating "Pending project-related approvals, both facilities are expected to be operational in late 2028 or 2029." (Release FY page:2). The 10-K expects fiscal 2027 capital expenditures of approximately 850.8 million including the Evansville plant, and development costs for the phosphate venture, with no financing plan stated (10-K page:76). The company also exited the Producer Ag joint venture on 2025-12-31 for working capital and cash, with no effect on the statement of operations (10-K page:159). The amount of the Producer Ag consideration is not supplied. Use of proceeds, sources and uses, and any new debt issue beyond the term loan are Not supplied because none is described.

fields.value: CHS Inc. entered fiscal 2026 with modest year-end leverage and finished with a very strong second half, when pretax income was 1,021,508 against 107,211 in the first half (C9). Derived EBITDA of 1,969,497 against total debt of 2,501,725 gives 1.27x at the 2026-08-31 balance sheet date, down from 2.12x a year earlier, and cash paid for interest of 167,057 is covered 11.79x. That picture is flattering in four ways that the base keeps in view. First, the EBITDA is our derivation (pretax income plus interest expense plus depreciation and amortization, including amortization of deferred major maintenance) because the company reports no EBITDA, and it includes 569,231 of equity income from joint ventures and affiliates. Second, nine-month operating earnings were a loss of 12,222 and the fourth quarter derived alone supplied most of the year, so the annual figure is dominated by one quarter. Third, the improvement is concentrated in one segment: Energy improved by 573,605, which exceeds the group improvement of 513,947 because Corporate and Services and Agronomy declined (C16). Fourth, working capital debt is seasonal: notes payable fell from 1,995,108 in February to 449,002 at year end, and on a last-twelve-months basis total debt over derived EBITDA was 2.57x in May 2026. The funded debt is long-dated private placement notes and a term loan with no single fiscal year through 2031 above 450,000, while the short-term funding includes securitization and repurchase facilities that now run only to 2027-08-25. Covenants are described only as minimum consolidated net worth and other financial ratios with compliance reported, so headroom is not measurable from these sources. The base supports statement-based credit work; it does not support covenant, ranking or recovery work.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CHS is a member-owned cooperative with no sponsor, no common stock and no pending acquisition, sponsor transaction or new debt issue, so the creditor questions are operating durability and distribution discipline rather than transaction risk. Its three reportable segments are Energy, Grains and Agronomy, with a financing and hedging arm and two minority joint ventures in Corporate and Services; the realignment to a product-line model took effect on 2025-09-01 and recast prior periods. Fiscal 2026 earnings leaned on three things the sources identify: strong refining spreads in Energy, partly cancelled by record renewable fuel compliance costs and helped by a small refinery exemption; oilseed crush and ethanol margins in Grains; and CF Nitrogen in Agronomy, a 7.86% interest that is the largest single source of equity income and sits in a venture CHS does not control. Against that, owner distributions are discretionary, the board cut cash patronage sharply in fiscal 2026 and has authorized an increase for fiscal 2027, and the preferred stock carries no vote. The company announced two large projects, a phosphate joint venture and a soybean plant, both pending approvals and not expected to operate before late 2028; their funding is not described. What the sources do not give is the legal layer: restricted payment capacity, covenant levels, guarantors and ranking. The annual report also contains a seasonality table whose fiscal 2026 fourth quarter share of pretax income (36%) and second quarter share (positive 15%) cannot be reconciled to the filed quarterly statements, which weakens any quarterly trend reading until resolved.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: No acquisition, sponsor transaction, merger or change of control is described in the sources, and the context lists no deal terms, so there is no transaction to summarize beyond the financing and project events below, each dated and classed by status. In fiscal 2026 the company issued no new notes: the debt table shows only the scheduled repayment of an 80,000 note and the sources state that "We repaid approximately $80.6 million and $331.6 million, respectively, of long-term debt consisting of scheduled debt maturities" for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2025 (10-K page:164). The one new long-term borrowing was the drawing of the revolving term loan: in the third quarter report the company states "we drew $300.0 million on our revolving term loan facility (the "Facility") for long-term capital planning purposes and utilized the proceeds to reduce short-term amounts outstanding" (10-Q Q3 page:13). That facility is fully drawn, its revolving period ends 2026-10-29 and it then becomes a nonrevolving term loan payable 2029-10-29 (10-K page:165); the scheduled reversion is a subsequent event after the fiscal year end that no later document confirms. On 2026-08-26 the securitization and repurchase facilities were extended to 2027-08-25 (10-K page:164). These are completed events, not proposals. Two announced projects are proposed and conditional: a phosphate production facility of nearly 450 million in Louisiana in a joint venture with OCP North America, and a soybean processing facility of approximately 700 million in Evansville, Wisconsin, with the release stating "Pending project-related approvals, both facilities are expected to be operational in late 2028 or 2029." (Release FY page:2). The 10-K expects fiscal 2027 capital expenditures of approximately 850.8 million including the Evansville plant, and development costs for the phosphate venture, with no financing plan stated (10-K page:76). The company also exited the Producer Ag joint venture on 2025-12-31 for working capital and cash, with no effect on the statement of operations (10-K page:159). The amount of the Producer Ag consideration is not supplied. Use of proceeds, sources and uses, and any new debt issue beyond the term loan are Not supplied because none is described.

Mechanically, the listed order places interest and preferred dividends first and owner returns after, but the order is a management statement and no contractual priority is supplied. The fiscal 2027 plan raises owner cash returns while capital expenditures are expected to rise to approximately 850.8 million from 463.3 million (10-K page:76), so fiscal 2027 cash demands combine growth capital, 168.7 million of preferred dividends, the owner distributions and 58,562 of scheduled debt maturities (CP-1), against a fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of 1,584,009 that CP-1 shows was swollen by working capital timing. No acquisition appetite is inferred from the single phosphate and soybean announcements. What the source set lacks for monitoring is logged in the gaps with severity.

This module synthesizes the fundamental credit view from the CP-1 financial base and the CP-1A business and transaction context, for fiscal 2026 (year ended 2026-08-31) in USD. fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CHS Inc. has a solid fundamental credit profile at the 2026-08-31 balance sheet date, but one that rests on volatile, commodity- and policy-driven earnings rather than steady cash flow. The strongest support is leverage of 1.27x total debt to derived EBITDA, cash interest cover of 11.79x, long-dated unsecured private placement debt with no fiscal year above USD 450.0 million through fiscal 2031, and USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver. The weakest point is earnings quality: Energy supplied the whole improvement, about USD 205.0 million came from a refinery exemption, and half of pretax income is equity income from ventures CHS does not control. What decides the outcome is whether refining spreads and nitrogen prices hold while about USD 1,536.1 million of identified fiscal 2027 cash demands are met, and whether covenants not yet seen leave room.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CHS Inc. entered fiscal 2027 with year-end total debt of USD 2,501.7 million against derived EBITDA of USD 1,969.5 million, a ratio of 1.27x, compared with 2.12x a year earlier (CP-1 C5). The improvement is real but partly seasonal, which the annual figure hides: the fall in total debt of USD 486.6 million, from USD 2,988.3 million, came entirely from notes payable, which fell by USD 703.5 million while long-term debt rose by USD 216.9 million (CP-1A D6), and on a last-twelve-months basis total debt over derived EBITDA was 2.53x, 2.92x and 2.57x at the three interim quarter ends (CP-1 C14). Leverage at the working capital peak is therefore 2.92x, not the 1.27x of the year-end balance sheet.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Earnings improved sharply and narrowly. Pretax income rose to USD 1,128.7 million from USD 614.8 million, and Energy alone moved from a loss of USD 19.0 million to earnings of USD 554.6 million, more than the group improvement of USD 513.9 million (CP-1 C16). Within Energy, the sources identify wider crack spreads and crude discounts, higher throughput, and a small refinery exemption benefit of approximately USD 205.0 million that management says only partially offsets total renewable fuel compliance costs and may not recur (CP-1A, 10-K page:64). Equity income was USD 569.2 million, 50.4% of pretax income (CP-2 E7), of which CF Nitrogen provided USD 406.3 million and USD 447.3 million of cash distributions. The fourth quarter derived from audited year less nine months carried USD 739.3 million of pretax income, and the annual report's own quarterly table disagrees with that split (CP-1A conflicts), so the phasing of the recovery is unverified while the annual totals stand.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Cash generation is strong in fiscal 2026 and not flattered by working capital. Operating cash flow was USD 1,584.0 million after a USD 184.0 million net working capital outflow (CP-2 E6), free cash flow after major maintenance was USD 1,052.5 million, and after preferred dividends and owner distributions it was USD 753.4 million (CP-1 C3, C4). This corrects CP-1A, which described operating cash flow as helped by working capital timing. In fiscal 2025 free cash flow after distributions was negative USD 1,120.9 million, so cash generation moved by USD 1,874.3 million between adjacent years (CP-2 E11).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fixed charges are covered but the margin depends on the earnings base. EBITDA covers cash interest plus preferred dividends 5.87x in fiscal 2026 against 4.47x in fiscal 2025, and on the narrower operating EBITDA measure the cover is 3.78x against 2.35x (CP-2 E1, E2). Adding operating lease liabilities of USD 237.5 million gives 1.39x leverage, and treating the preferred stock at its redemption value of USD 2,273.3 million as a debt-like fixed claim gives 2.42x (CP-2 E3, E4), an analytical adjustment and not a statement of legal ranking.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The forward funding position is adequate but not abundant. Identified fiscal 2027 demands of USD 1,536.1 million comprise capital expenditures of USD 850.8 million, major maintenance of USD 41.8 million, preferred dividends of USD 168.7 million, owner cash returns of USD 315.0 million on the filing figures, scheduled long-term debt maturities of USD 58.6 million and interest on long-term debt of USD 101.3 million (CP-2 E5). That is close to fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,584.0 million, so a repeat of fiscal 2026 funds the plan almost exactly, and any shortfall would fall on the USD 2,800.0 million revolver, which is USD 1.40 of capacity for every USD 1.00 of the largest quarter-end notes payable balance of USD 1,995.1 million (CP-2 E8), or on the board's discretion over owner payments. Two announced projects of USD 450 million and USD 700 million are additional and unfunded in the sources.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: What cannot be concluded: covenant headroom, because the net worth and ratio tests are described but no level is printed; the effect of letters of credit on revolver availability; structural position of creditors, because guarantors and security are not stated; and ratings and market pricing, which are out of scope.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. First, balance sheet and liquidity: year-end leverage of 1.27x, USD 263.6 million of unrestricted cash and USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver to 2028-04-21 give CHS Inc. a liquidity base of about USD 3,063.6 million gross of letters of credit that are not supplied (CP-1, CP-2 E9). Second, debt profile: the long-term debt is unsecured private placement notes and a USD 300.0 million term loan, with USD 899.3 million, 44.9% of the total, maturing in the five fiscal years to 2031 and the largest single year at USD 450.0 million (CP-2 E10). Third, a discretionary distribution lever: the board decides the cash portion of patronage and the level of equity redemptions, and cash patronage paid fell from USD 300.4 million to USD 30.0 million between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026, so a stress case can release cash without a default event (CP-1A). Fourth, diversification across Energy, Grains and Agronomy, a financing arm and two minority joint ventures. Fifth, demonstrated cash support from CF Nitrogen of USD 447.3 million of distributions in fiscal 2026.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. First, thin and volatile operating earnings: operating earnings were USD 591.9 million on revenues of USD 39,231.2 million, a margin of 1.5%, and USD 90.8 million in fiscal 2025, so pretax income relies on equity income and other income (CP-1). Second, policy and spread dependence in Energy, where the largest blending obligation ever issued, open-market RIN purchases and a refinery exemption that may not recur all decide margin. Third, concentration: CF Nitrogen provides 71% of equity income (CP-1A D3), a non-controlled venture whose distributions follow nitrogen prices. Fourth, a working capital model that takes quarter-end leverage to 2.92x and ties up large inventory and receivables, with derivative liabilities of USD 546.6 million at year end against USD 178.0 million a year earlier, a mechanic for margin and liquidity calls if commodity prices spike, which the sources do not quantify (CP-1). Fifth, unverifiable structure and covenants: no agreement is supplied. Sixth, growth capital: expected capital expenditure of USD 850.8 million in fiscal 2027 against USD 463.3 million in fiscal 2026 plus two projects with no stated funding. Seventh, a small related-party exposure of USD 10.3 million past due from a director's farm, under Audit Committee-approved terms (CP-1A).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: CP-1A stated that fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of 1,584,009 was swollen by working capital timing. The cash flow statement shows the opposite: receivables, inventories, payables and other lines together used USD 184.0 million in fiscal 2026 and USD 464.4 million in fiscal 2025 (CP-2 E6; 10-K page:146), so fiscal 2026 operating cash flow was not flattered by a working capital release. CP-1A's related remark that free cash flow swings with working capital is true of the year-on-year change only in part: the swing between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026 also reflects higher earnings and lower capital spending. No other statement in CP-0, CP-1 or CP-1A is changed. The CP-1A conflict on the quarterly share table and the CP-0 and CP-1 point on fiscal 2027 redemptions (USD 165.0 million on the filing, against up to USD 150 million in the release) are carried; this module uses the filing.
